Q: How can I generate human-friendly numeric scale values between two float64 values in Go? A:

A useful approach is to first calculate the ideal mathematical step and then round that step up to a human-friendly value from the sequence:

1 × 10ⁿ
2 × 10ⁿ
5 × 10ⁿ
10 × 10ⁿ

This is the same general idea commonly used for chart axis ticks.

func Steps(from, to float64, maxCount int) *util.ArrayList[float64] {
    step := step(from, to, maxCount)
    if step == 0 {
        return util.ArrayListOf(from)
    }

    start := StripFloat(math.Floor(from/step) * step)
    end := StripFloat(math.Ceil(to/step) * step)

    result := util.NewArrayList[float64]()
    for v := start; v <= end; v = StripFloat(v + step) {
        result.Add(v)
    }
    return result
}

func step(from, to float64, maxCount int) float64 {
    if maxCount <= 1 {
        return to - from
    }
    if from == to {
        return 0
    }

    rangeVal := math.Abs(to - from)
    rawStep := rangeVal / float64(maxCount-1)

    pow := math.Pow10(int(math.Floor(math.Log10(rawStep))))
    norm := rawStep / pow

    var nice float64
    switch {
    case norm <= 1:
        nice = 1
    case norm <= 2:
        nice = 2
    case norm <= 5:
        nice = 5
    default:
        nice = 10
    }

    return nice * pow
}

func StripFloat(v float64) float64 {
    return math.Round(v*1e12) / 1e12
}

The important part is the normalization of the raw step.

For:

from := 3.2
to := 9.6
maxCount := 6

the range is:

9.6 - 3.2 = 6.4

With six requested values there are five intervals, so the ideal step is:

6.4 / (6 - 1) = 1.28

The order of magnitude is obtained with:

pow := math.Pow10(int(math.Floor(math.Log10(rawStep))))

For 1.28:

log10(1.28) ≈ 0.107
floor(...)   = 0
10⁰          = 1

The raw step is then normalized relative to that power of ten:

norm = 1.28 / 1 = 1.28

The next suitable value in the 1, 2, 5, 10 sequence is 2, so:

step = 2 × 1 = 2

The requested range is then expanded to multiples of that step:

start := math.Floor(3.2/2) * 2
end := math.Ceil(9.6/2) * 2

which gives:

start = 2
end   = 10

and therefore:

[2 4 6 8 10]

The useful property of normalizing the value first is that exactly the same logic works at any decimal magnitude.

For example, if the raw step is:

0.00128

then:

pow  = 0.001
norm = 1.28
nice = 2
step = 0.002

If the raw step is:

1280

then:

pow  = 1000
norm = 1.28
nice = 2
step = 2000

So the selection logic itself never needs to know whether it is dealing with thousandths, units, thousands, or millions.

StripFloat is used when calculating the boundaries and repeatedly adding the step because binary floating-point arithmetic can otherwise produce values such as:

0.1
0.2
0.30000000000000004
0.4

Rounding to a fixed precision after each addition prevents those artifacts from accumulating for the intended numeric range:

func StripFloat(v float64) float64 {
    return math.Round(v*1e12) / 1e12
}

Q: How do I proxy upstream to Burp? A:

The following may help;

Firstly, configure Burp to listen on 0.0.0.0:8080 (all interfaces) or on the host interface.

Secondly, determine the IP address of your host machine as seen by HTTP Toolkit /Android.

Thirdly, configure HTTP Toolkit to use upstream proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 to

http://<host-ip>:8080

Lastly, configure the host machine firewall to allow connections to port 8080.

Afterwards, you can make a request to test whether everything is working.

For HTTPS traffic, you have installed the Burp CA certificate in Android, so that is sorted out.

Q: Implementing a custom comparer that treats the numbers as integers rather than strings A:

Microsoft sorts numbers as text by default

No it doesn't, and your code doesn't show anything different. Disproving this is easy as this C# fiddle and this DB fiddle show:

var numbers=  new List<int> { 1, 11, 2, 3, 10 };
numbers.Sort();
Console.WriteLine(String.Join(",",numbers));
-----
1,2,3,10,11

create table Numbers(num int);
insert into Numbers
values (1), (11), (2), (3), (10);

select * from Numbers order by num;
-----
1
2
3
10
11

All database applications (in any language) depend on numbers getting sorted as numbers, so if what you claims were true, everyone would notice. You'll have to provide actual code, the actual table schema and actual data so others can replicate this extraordinary claim.

Chances are that the application itself stores numbers as strings, which is an application bug. Perhaps you're actually storing a week number as string?

Or perhaps you didn't use an ORDER BY clause? Table rows have no inherent order. The database (any database, not just SQL Server) will return rows in the cheapest way if you don't use an ORDER BY clause.

You didn't post your table or any query that compares anything, so it's impossible to guess what's going on.

Q: Is it possible for two cases in a switch statement to execute common code, followed by code specific to each case? A:

Switch-case works in this fashion: The control is transferred from the switch statement to the first match and then all the statements are executed(including those from other cases) until a break statement is encountered. This behavior is known as fallthrough.

So, Whenever this case is caught in switch,

case 'foo':
case 'bar':
    console.log('its foo or bar');

This case is always called:

 case 'foo':
    console.log('its foo');

The reason is that there is no break statement after the first snippet. So, the control goes on executing the statements until it encounters a break statement.

Q: git working on two branches simultaneously A:

Git 2.5+ (Q2 2015) supports this feature!

If you have a git repo cool-app, cd to root (cd cool-app), run git worktree add ../cool-app-feature-A feature/A. This checks out the branch feature/A in it's own new dedicated directory, cool-app-feature-A.

That replaces an older script contrib/workdir/git-new-workdir, with a more robust mechanism where those "linked" working trees are actually recorded in the main repo new $GIT_DIR/worktrees folder (so that work on any OS, including Windows).

Again, once you have cloned a repo (in a folder like /path/to/myrepo), you can add worktrees for different branches in different independent paths (/path/to/br1, /path/to/br2), while having those working trees linked to the main repo history (no need to use a --git-dir option anymore)

See more at "Multiple working directories with Git?".

And once you have created a worktree, you can move or remove it (with Git 2.17+, Q2 2018).

majorgear asks in the comments:

Can you clarify the process? Do you clone a repository first, and then run worktree commands? Where are the new directories created? Under the directory created by the git clone command or elsewhere?

If you are starting from a remote repository, you clone it once.
If you already have the repository locally, you can skip that step.

For instance (for exisiting branches):

cd /path/to/parent
git clone <repository-url> cool-app
cd cool-app

git worktree add ../cool-app-feature-A feature/A
git worktree add ../cool-app-feature-B feature/B

That gives you:

/path/to/parent/
├── cool-app/                 # main worktree created by git clone
├── cool-app-feature-A/       # linked worktree, branch feature/A
└── cool-app-feature-B/       # linked worktree, branch feature/B

The directory is created at the <path> passed to git worktree add.
Here, ../cool-app-feature-A means "one directory above cool-app", so the new worktrees are siblings of the original clone, not subdirectories of it.

That path does not have to be next to the original clone: it can be another relative or absolute path.
The important point is that those directories are linked worktrees of the same repository, not independent clones. They share the repository's Git objects and refs, but each worktree has its own checked-out files, HEAD, and index.

That is also the direct answer to the original question, which asks how to work on several branches simultaneously without copying the whole repository somewhere else: clone once, then create one linked worktree for each branch you want to have checked out at the same time.

Note: git worktree add ../cool-app-feature-A feature/A is enough for an existing branch, but if you want to create a new branch at the same time, use -b <new-branch>:

git worktree add -b feature/A ../cool-app-feature-A

That creates feature/A, starting from HEAD by default, and checks it out in the new worktree.
You can also specify the starting point:

git worktree add -b feature/A ../cool-app-feature-A main

There is also a shorthand when the branch name you want is the basename of the new directory. As documented for git worktree add, if the branch does not already exist, git worktree add ../feat-branch-1 can create a new branch named feat-branch-1 from HEAD automatically. Using -b is more explicit, and is needed when the branch name cannot simply be guessed that way.

Also, once a linked worktree has been created, do not move its directory with the filesystem alone. Git keeps administrative information associating that path with the worktree. Use git worktree move <worktree> <new-path> instead:

git worktree move ../cool-app-feature-A ../somewhere-else/cool-app-feature-A

If a linked worktree has already been moved manually, git worktree repair can re-establish the connection between the repository and its new location. That is a only a recovery mechanism: git worktree move is the command to use when you want to move an existing worktree.

Q: AssertionError: Burger is not open. class='burger' A:

The likely cause might be this line in their capabilities: options.set_capability("pageLoadStrategy", "none").

pageLoadStrategy: "none" tells the driver to return control immediately after navigation starts, without waiting for the page to finish loading. On a local desktop browser this often goes unnoticed because pages load fast enough that by the time your next command runs, things are ready anyway. On an Android emulator running Chrome, page load and JS execution are noticeably slower, so your test is very likely trying to click the burger menu and assert it opened before the page's JS (and the menu's click handler) has actually finished initializing.

That matches your symptom: it's not that the element isn't found, it's that interacting with it doesn't produce the expected state change, which is the classic signature of racing page load rather than a locator or logic problem.

Two ways to fix it:

  1. Add an explicit wait before opening the menu, waiting for a reliable "page ready" indicator (a specific element you know only appears after full load) rather than relying on pageLoadStrategy timing.

  2. Or switch pageLoadStrategy to "normal" for this specific flow and see if the flakiness disappears, that confirms the diagnosis before you commit to explicit waits everywhere.

I'd lean toward explicit waits long-term since mobile browser automation is inherently slower and more variable than desktop, and pageLoadStrategy: "none" combined with no wait is a common source of exactly this kind of intermittent failure.

Q: How to save a colored JPG image to the Milvus database? A:

I tried to use potrace

Be aware that Milvus is a vector database, which means that it stores "vectors" in that specific sense. They have nothing to do with a vector image format such as SVG.

Q: Why can't `terra` project a raster when I change the extent's xmin? A:

This message

Warning message:
Too many points (441 out of 441) failed to transform, unable to compute output bounds. (GDAL error 1)

is expected if none of the input data can be projected to the requested CRS, because the output CRS does not cover the geographic area of the input data.

In your example, that is not the case, and it work fine with current terra and R on windows (you do not show the output of library(terra)

library(terra)
#terra 1.9.34
 
# Works fine when x range is -90 to -80:
a <- rast(ncols=40, nrows=40, xmin=-90, xmax=-80, ymin=25, ymax=26, crs="EPSG:4269")
project(a, "EPSG:4326")
#class       : SpatRaster
#size        : 6, 56, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#resolution  : 0.1776583, 0.1776583  (x, y)
#extent      : -90, -80.05113, 24.93405, 26  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)

# Throws an error when x range is -85 to -80:
b <- rast(ncols=40, nrows=40, xmin=-85, xmax=-80, ymin=25, ymax=26, crs="EPSG:4269")
project(b, "EPSG:4326")
#class       : SpatRaster
#size        : 11, 55, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#resolution  : 0.09013871, 0.09013871  (x, y)
#extent      : -85, -80.04237, 25.00848, 26  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)

(related to your earlier example: changing the CRS from lon/lat NAD83 (EPSG:4269) to lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) does not really require any computation, they are effectively the same). So you can also do

crs(b) <- "EPSG:4326"

This is not the case if you want to use Pseudo-Mercator (EPSG:3857).

Q: Why is rep movsb slow for overlapping forward memmove, and why does libc use it? A:

In the quoted case (your measurements), there are two independent thresholds:

  1. With n = +5, the call is memmove(v, v + 5, size), the destination is below the source, so a forward copy is correct, but the ranges overlap with a distance of only five bytes.
  2. In your VCRuntime test, 8191 bytes uses a vector loop, while 8193 selects rep movsb. Thus 8192 is a dispatch threshold of that library build, not a hardware boundary (microsoft/STL #5506).

Your measurements show that on some CPUs, including Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, and the Alder Lake P-core, forward rep movsb is exceptionally slow when source and destination differ by 1 through 63 bytes. The architectural definition guarantees the result, but not how the fast-string engine implements it. In my opinion, the measurements are consistent with a dependency-related close-overlap slow path, but that mechanism is an inference rather than a published fact, saying that the instruction necessarily copies byte-by-byte or internally uses 64-byte chunks would go beyond the evidence. Intel also documents significant performance degradation for backward rep movsb (DF=1) (Intel Optimization Manual section 3.7.6.3, quoted in the earlier answer). Glibc, for example, instead branches to a backward vector path when dst > src.

Intel's optimization reference manual, volume 1 lists the favourable conditions together: forward direction, source and destination aligned to 16 bytes, a length that is a multiple of 64, and regions that do not overlap. These four are optimal-performance conditions, not a promise that missing any one always selects a byte-at-a-time path. The software developer's manual, volumes 2A to 2D specifies the repeated MOVSB result but does not specify the fast-string engine's internal width.

You observed the severe case on Ice Lake, Tiger Lake, and the Alder Lake P-core, but not on Skylake/Coffee Lake or the Alder Lake E-core. Your tests do not establish an exhaustive CPU list. Intel introduced FSRM with Ice Lake. Glibc uses it as a conservative indicator for applying this workaround on Intel CPUs, not as a guarantee that every FSRM implementation has the same penalty. The exact behaviour is microarchitectural.

Libraries use rep movsb because it can be fast for sufficiently large non-overlapping forward copies, with compact code and no separate tail loop (discussion and measurements). Intel documents about a 35-cycle startup cost for the cited pre-FSRM ERMS implementations, making rep movsb unattractive for short copies. FSRM and later implementations need not have the same startup behaviour. The crossover is CPU-, alignment-, cache-, and library-dependent, and sufficiently large copies can beat some vector loops under favourable conditions, but measurements on one CPU are not guarantees for another. In this runtime-sized benchmark, the compilers call memmove. On Linux, the installed libc therefore selects the instruction sequence, not Clang or GCC. Compilers may still inline or transform other calls when the size and alignment are known.

Yes, the library should avoid this corner case. Glibc added exactly such a check: on Intel CPUs with FSRM it avoids rep movsb when the source/destination distance modulo 4 GiB is 1 through 63 bytes and falls back to its vector path (glibc change, the check lives in memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S). In the accepted answer, you report finding an equivalent less-than-64-byte-distance check without a CPU gate in MSVC's v14.50 CRT, which Microsoft ships with Visual Studio 2026. The glibc change includes benchmark evidence that gating the workaround avoids regressions on Intel processors without FSRM. Both implementations retain the ordinary rep movsb path while excluding this pathological distance case, although you did not provide equivalent before-and-after benchmark data for MSVC in your initial question.

A caller that controls both pointers can rule the corner case out structurally instead of checking distance. FastMM4-AVX, my fork of the FastMM4 allocator originally written by Pierre le Riche, compares an already tail-adjusted count against a 2048-byte tuning threshold in its AVX-512 move routine. Because the routine has already removed the eight-byte tail, that comparison corresponds to a 2056-byte full block. No distance check guards its rep movsb. As far as I can tell from its intended allocator use, the allocator calls this routine for reallocation copies only after obtaining a distinct destination block, so those particular source and destination allocations cannot overlap; establishing that property from the repository alone requires following the routine's call sites as well as inspecting the assembly.

A Reported AMD Case at Power-of-Two-Spaced Addresses

A comment on this answer asks whether FastMM4-AVX works around a related AMD problem, memcpy running 10 to 40 times slower when dst-src is close. Per microsoft/STL issue 5658, the trigger is dst - src close to a power of two, in either direction, with count at least 4096 bytes on x86 or 8193 on x64. The issue reproduces on some AMD systems under Windows and Linux and is gone on newer Ubuntu combinations, so the mechanism and the affected-CPU list remain open. CPython hit the same pattern multiplying lists of 2^k + 1 elements.

The ranges do not overlap at that distance; the small quantity is the excess above a power-of-two separation, and the 1-to-63-byte distance checks in glibc and MSVC do not cover it. The 8193-byte boundary sits just above the 8192-byte VCRuntime dispatch threshold measured at the top of this answer, pointing at a REP MOVS path without proving one. Separately, glibc measured rep movsb about 20 times slower than vector loops for unfavourably aligned copies on Zen 3 and Zen 4 and stopped preferring ERMS there (measurements, glibc change), a caution against reading AMD's ERMS and FSRM bits as performance promises, though that alignment trigger is not shown identical to the distance trigger here.

FastMM4-AVX library has no vendor gate and no such distance test, so nothing works around the reported condition. The non-overlap argument only excludes the close-overlap case, and separately allocated blocks can still land at the reported spacing. Whether the library is affected is unproven: on Win64, MoveWithErmsNoAVX uses rep movsb only for 65-to-192-byte FSRM copies and a 64-byte-aligned rep movsq above 192 bytes, while the reported x64 trigger begins at 8193 bytes; the Unix x86-64 routine does use rep movsb directly, and no reproduction against the library has been published. A benchmark of the library's routines on affected Zen hardware does not exist yet; without one, a vendor gate, a distance mask, or any other fix would be a guesstimate.
